items.title: WTF are evals? How to test agents and the software they use
items.summary: Agents are now users of software, doing work on people's behalf. Whether you're building the agent or the software it uses (API, CLI, MCP server, SDK), evals give you a way to measure how well that work gets done.Agents probably missed your launch video and billboard on Highway 101, but they still go through the same funnel a human does to find and use a product: , , , and .DiscoverySelectionAccessSuccessYou can build evals for any stage of this funnel. Here, we’ll focus on the final stage, : whether the agent completes the user’s task correctly.SuccessThat's more difficult to check than it sounds. An agent can place a “successful” order for a hot latte when the user asked for an iced one. The request worked, so the logs in your Observability stack look fine. And because LLM outputs vary between runs, one good manual test can’t tell you whether a fix worked. You need to repeat the same tasks and grade the outcomes, before and after the change.That’s what an eval can do for you. Here’s how we build one.If a test asks “did it work?” an eval asks “how often does it work, and how well?” You give an agent a task, grade the outcome, and aggregate the results across repeated attempts. We group agentic software tests by how many LLM calls they typically need: deterministic tests (0), one-turn evals (1), and E2E evals (2+ across a whole task). This has turned out to be a great proxy for the effort to build them, the time they take to run, and the cost of running them. Just like in , the cheap and fast tests should make up the bulk of your test suite. the practical test pyramidTo use the pyramid, start with the problem you want to catch and pick the lowest tier that can catch it. For , that's the top. A one-turn eval checks a single decision, like which command the agent runs first. But  depends on the whole sequence of steps (e.g. search for cafes → filter on user criteria → place the latte order). Each one can look reasonable on its own, and the agent can still get the wrong outcome. SuccessSuccessAn E2E eval lets the agent work through the whole task in an environment, then checks whether the final result meets the user’s requirements. You’ve probably seen a few already; most popular coding benchmarks, like  and , are E2E evals.SWE-benchTerminal-BenchSay you own SF Beans, an API for ordering coffee in San Francisco. One of the best ways to give agents access to your service is through a CLI, so you’re shipping .sfbeansHere’s a typical request from one of your customers:Here’s what  knows at 8:30am:sfbeansHere’s what you could test at each layer of the pyramid for :sfbeansWe’ll build the coffee eval with , an open-source framework from the creators of Terminal-Bench that runs agents in containers, checks results, and records their actions.HarborHere are the terms we’ll use:Building E2E evals for everything isn’t practical. With traditional software, you can aim for 100% test coverage. With agents, the surface you’d need to cover is everything an LLM  do with your product, and even figuring out where that ends is hard (see ). mightthe jagged frontierStart with one outcome your users care about, narrow enough to evaluate with a handful of tasks. You’ll usually find that goal in one of three places:For example, your goal might be to:We looked in all three places for :sfbeansThat gives us our goal:Here are the metrics we use most for E2E agent evals:SuccessEfficiency (measured on successful trials only)Our goal is to get every order right in every trial. Once we build and run the eval in Steps 3 and 4, here’s what five trials of Claude Code + Opus 5.5 ( on ) on the iced latte order could look like:anthropic/claude-opus-5.5AI GatewayWhat the numbers mean:So does Opus work? Its 99% pass@5 says yes. Its 8% pass^5 says a user who orders this every weekday gets at least one wrong coffee in 92% of weeks. Both numbers are right. They just answer different questions: pass@5 asks whether the agent  get the order right, and pass^5 asks whether it gets it right .canevery timeWhich metric matters most depends on what a failure costs your user. Someone ordering their morning coffee doesn’t get a retry. If the agent orders a hot latte, or one that’s ready after their train leaves, they’ve paid for the wrong coffee and started their day annoyed. They need it right every morning, so  optimizes for pass^5.sfbeansOther products are more forgiving, because a failed attempt is cheap and gets caught before it matters:Overall averages can hide a task that fails frequently, so always inspect results per task. And with only five trials, 100% means “no failures seen yet,” not “never fails.”In Step 1, we set a goal for the eval: increase how often agents order the exact drink the user asked for. But an agent can’t attempt a goal. It needs a task: one concrete request, drawn from what your users actually ask for.Pick tasks hard enough that you learn something from running them.
